items.title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
items.content: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns. To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models. Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails. At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected. More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Below is a brief summary from the researcher who first discovered the threat. We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. items.title: Import AI 480: Self-sustaining space economies; AI for science progress, and Meta builds perfect hands for a superintelligence
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI Science startup converts a quantum conjecture into a theorem: …An evocative taste of the singularity… In the same way a few years ago it went from remarkable to unremarkable to see computers gain the ability to identify objects in images, we’re now in an era where it’s rapidly going from remarkable to unremarkable for computers to extend the bounds of human knowledge. The latest example comes from Physical Superintelligence, an AI science startup which has proved a longstanding quantum computing conjecture. What they did: “Open since 2008, the conjecture of Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis concerns when quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones. Now, a research system developed internally at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), running a non-public Anthropic model, found a proof for it, settling one of the most fundamental questions in quantum computing,” the startup writes. “The system had a complete proof of the conjecture during the third day of the run, and Lean, a proof assistant in which a computer checks every step, accepted it. We then set the system to work on related open problems. Along the way, the system improved the result twice, and Lean accepted the final version.” Why this matters – we are in the singularity : As I said in my speech at the IMF ( #477 ), I believe we’re in the early stages of the singularity, defined as the period when the rate of technological and scientific progress exceeds the rate at which we humans can parse out and make sense of it. Research like this is a taste of what that means; mostly automated synthetic researchers extending the frontier of knowledge, spitting out results which need to then be understood by humans. items.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
items.content: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting bille…

items.title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
items.content: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. As Almeida quipped during his presentation, “you get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” “And if you can't tell which is which, how the fuck are you going to automate anything,” he added. Almeida ended with an impassioned plea to “automate ev…

items.title: Jensen Out, MATCH Act In?
items.content: Jordan Schneider, Dylan Patel, and Jordan Nanos of SemiAnalysis record an emergency pod after Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO. We discuss: Why Jensen’s exit could become cover for “really stupid laws” — and why Dylan backs the MATCH Act but thinks RASA is a mistake. The game theory of remote access: renting compute to Chinese firms as margin capture and a kill switch, versus closing the Malaysia loophole outright. “Flip the table”: why equipment controls beat chip and model controls, and how close Huawei’s silicon now is. Why no American lab has out-built Kimi or DeepSeek in open models. Nvidia without Jensen: talent retention, Rubin and Feynman execution risk, and who should run the company. Colette Kress’s exposure, Supermicro and Megaspeed, and a fight over whether this amounts to the “nationalization” of Nvidia. Listen now on your favorite podcast app . Jensen Resigns Jordan Nanos: Hey, Dylan. Hey, Jordan. Did you guys hear the CEO of the world’s largest and most important company just resigned? Dylan Patel: No. Jordan Nanos: Are you serious? What could possibly have led to that? Well, there are allegations of some pretty serious conduct violations. Apparently you can’t sleep with your subordinates and keep your job. items.title: Piggybacking to the Frontier
items.content: American data companies like Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing are selling roughly half a billion dollars worth of data to Chinese AI labs. A chunk of that data comes in the form of reinforcement learning (RL) environments, which labs use to post-train their models to make them excel at specific domains like coding, cyber, finance, law, and bio. Post-training, and especially RL, is one of the most important indicators of the final performance of a model. Whenever a new model within a single generation drops, the advances from the previous release are entirely due to post-training. The difference between Opus 5 to Opus 5.5, or from GPT 5.5 to GPT 5.6, is not due to a new pre-training run. Since they have the same base model, the capability gains come from researchers teaching the model to get better at specific domains. The phenomenon of American companies arming Chinese labs with the data that enables this RL should set off alarms for policymakers and those invested in the U.S.-China AI race: American companies are helping Chinese labs develop better models, and we were able to find at least nine who do so. But the business relationships between data vendors and Chinese labs are more complicated than that single hawkish line, and today, we’re diving into what’s going on. We’ll cover: What it means to sell an RL environment and how it differs from distillation The current ecosystem of China-tied data vendors To what extent American companies are selling RL environments to China Whether this is a problem that needs fixing What RL Does and Doesn’t Look Like Example RL Flows RL environments are essentially simulated worlds in which a model can train to improve its performance at specific tasks or environments. As an example, a model developer may want their model to get better at creating PowerPoint slides with pleasant aesthetics and clear text. items.title: Why the Cyberpocalypse Might Hit China Harder
items.content: Chang Che is a writer and contributor to the New Yorker . In August, researchers at a California security firm used an OpenAI model to find a software bug in PHP, a programming language that undergird some seventy per cent of the world’s websites, including Wikipedia and WordPress. They alerted PHP’s developers, who quietly began working on a fix. By late October, the fix was ready, but before they could alert the world, the break-in attempts had begun. Days earlier, Amazon detected someone trying to hack into its servers; attacks code began circulating online. Some governments and companies began pulling websites down, rather than risk a security breach. One security firm described the flaws as some of the worst ever found in PHP, “and arguably in software history.” Before AI, the internet might have looked, to a hacker, like a worn-out bug screen. You could discern some holes with a keen eye, and that knowledge was reliably asymmetric—others probably didn’t know about the holes you found. Moreover, tunneling through the holes undetected took months or years of human labor, talent, and money. Now, with AI, the internet looks more like a block of Swiss cheese: the holes are obvious, anyone can, or will, see them, and the time and cost it takes to exploit these software flaws have plunged alarmingly fast . According to Google’s incident response team , the average time it takes for cyber criminals to exploit a new vulnerability is -7 days, meaning hacking attempts are “routinely occurring before a patch is even released.” A China Central Television (CCTV) feature about the PHP vulnerability discovered by cybersecurity firm Calif, with the aid of OpenAI models. Source . Hackers refer to unbeknownst software bugs like PHP as “zero-days” because a defender has had zero days to protect themselves upon its discovery. Once a hacker discovers a zero-day in, say, iOS software, every iPhone user is potentially…
